posts.author: Dr. Mohamed Abdellaziz Hmad
posts.title: The SouqThat Had No Contracts
posts.body:
I was young enough that the souq felt enormous, and old enough to understand that my

father had brought me there for a reason, even if he never said it out loud.

We would leave early, when Ksar Hellal was still waking up. The town was already humming

by then. In some places a town wakes up with birds or church bells; in ours it woke up with

machines. Somewhere behind the walls, looms were already clattering, a steady metallic

rhythm that you stop hearing after a few days and start missing the moment you leave.

The streets smelled of strong coffee, warm bread, and under everything the dry, dusty,

slightly sweet smell of cotton. If you grow up in a textile town, that smell becomes your

smell of home.

My father walked with his hands behind his back, in no hurry, nodding at people left and

right. In a town like ours, a walk to the market was never just a walk. Every few steps

someone called his name, and every call meant a handshake, a question about the family, a

comment on the weather, a joke. I learned much later that this was already business.

Nobody was selling anything yet, but everyone was being seen, remembered, and

measured.

The old souq opened in front of us like a different country.

The first thing that hit me was the sound. Dozens of voices overlapped in Tunisian dialect,

shouting prices, laughing, arguing in the half-serious way that people argue when they

already know how the argument will end. Carts rattled over uneven stones. Somewhere a

metal shutter screeched upward. Someone dropped a crate, someone else cursed it, and a

third person laughed.

Then the colors. Thread was everywhere, in cones and spools and tangled hanks, stacked

in open crates along the walls. Deep indigo next to bright red, mustard yellow next to

bleached white, and a dull grey that I later learned was the color of undyed cotton thread,

which meant it was still waiting to become something. Bales of raw cotton sat near the

entrances, wrapped in rough sacking, some already torn open so the buyers could see

what was inside. White tufts drifted through the air like small slow snowflakes and settled

on shoulders, on hair, on the dark wool of the men's jackets. By noon, everyone in the souq

wore a light dusting of cotton and nobody seemed to notice.

And the men. I remember their hands more than their faces. Thick, cracked, stained at the

fingertips from dye and oil. Those hands never stopped moving. They picked up a tuft of

cotton and pulled it apart slowly, testing the length of the fiber. They rolled a thread

between thumb and finger, held it up to the light, sometimes even brought it close to their

nose. They squeezed a bale with a flat palm, as if checking the heartbeat of an animal.

There were no instruments in sight, no scales with digital screens, no laboratory reports.

These men had spent thirty or forty years touching the same material, and their fingertips

had become better sensors than any machine I would encounter later in my life.

I stood beside my father and watched one of those moments that I now think about

constantly.

A merchant, a heavy man with a grey mustache and a tarboush pushed back on his head,

was talking to a buyer who had come from a workshop a few streets away. They talked

about the cotton, about the season, about someone's cousin who had just returned from

abroad. Ten minutes passed before a single price was mentioned. Then the merchant said

a number, the buyer clicked his tongue and said a lower one, the merchant looked at the

sky as if offended by the insult, and the buyer laughed. They met somewhere in the

middle. The buyer put out his hand, the merchant took it, and that was it.

Please understand what had just happened. A truckload of cotton, worth more than many

families earned in a year, had just been sold. And there was no paper. No signature, no

stamp, no lawyer, no notary, no written terms. Nobody had said when payment was due, or

if they had, it was a loose phrase like "after the Eid" or "when you've sold the first batch."

The buyer's men started loading the bales onto a cart while the two men were already

drinking tea together and talking about something else.

I asked my father quietly, the way children ask the questions adults forget to ask: "What if

he doesn't pay?"

My father smiled without looking at me. "Then he won't buy again. From anyone."

At the time, it sounded like a simple answer. It took me years, and a PhD, to see how

complete it was.

Because that was the whole system. The contract was the man's name. The court was the

town. If a buyer failed to pay, the story would travel through the souq before he reached

home: at the coffee shops, in the workshops, between the looms, over the Friday meal. By

the following week, no merchant would sell him thread on credit. By the following month,

even people who had never met him would know his name and the story attached to it. In

a town where everyone is connected to everyone, a broken promise is never a private

matter. It is public property and a permanent record.

And so the most remarkable thing about the old souq was how rarely anyone broke a

promise. Not because people were saints, but because the cost was so high and so

certain that honesty became the cheapest strategy.

I watched men build fortunes this way. Quiet men in simple clothes who owned

workshops with dozens of machines, who started out buying one small lot of cotton on

credit from a merchant who trusted their word, and who paid it back early, every single

time, until one day that merchant offered them ten lots instead of one. No bank had

assessed them. No analyst had studied their risk. A reputation had grown slowly, like a

tree, and one day it was strong enough to carry real weight.

Years later, I would sit in university rooms and learn the vocabulary of what I had seen as a

child: informal institutions, relational contracting, social capital, trust-based governance. I

would read academic papers analyzing exactly what those men did by instinct. I

remember a moment in a lecture when a professor presented these ideas as exotic

discoveries, and I smiled quietly, because I had watched them happen with cotton dust in

my hair.

But the souq taught me something else too, something no lecture covered, and I only

understood it when I began working for a business owner back in Tunisia.

I won't name him, and I won't say what exactly he sold. What matters is the pattern. He

had found one thing that worked. One product, one way of buying, one way of selling, one

circle of people he trusted. He tried it, it succeeded, and from that day on it became

untouchable. Every idea that did not look like the original formula was treated with

suspicion. Every new person who came with a different method was welcomed politely at

the door and quietly kept at a distance. It wasn't arrogance, exactly. It was fear, wearing

the clothes of experience. He had seen what works, and he saw no reason ever to risk it.

I recognized it immediately, because I had seen it before in the souq. The same trust that

made the system so strong also made it closed. The fortune was built inside a bubble, and

the bubble protected it, and the bubble also decided who could never come in. Outsiders,

new ideas, new models, young people with different questions: all of them stayed outside,

politely, forever.

Sitting in his office, watching this, something settled inside me.

I felt no desire to become him. I admired him, genuinely. I respected the instinct that had

built what he had built. But when I imagined running a business of my own, I felt nothing.

No pull, no hunger, no restless itch to be the name on the door. What I felt instead was a

pull toward the empty chair beside him. I wanted to be the person who could see what he

could not see from inside the bubble, who could translate his instincts into something he

could examine, strengthen, and pass on. I wanted to build around the fortune, not

necessarily to own it.

And that's the separation I want to leave you with, because I think we rarely say it out

loud. Our culture quietly insists that everyone with talent and ambition must end up as an

owner. Nobody tells you that being born to run a business and being born to work with

one are two different callings, and that neither is smaller than the other. The souq in Ksar

Hellal needed both: the merchant who held the word of the whole market in his hand, and

the people around him who made that word travel, grow, and survive.

It took me years to accept which of the two I was. It's why I study how businesses are

designed, why I sit with owners and ask them questions, and why I am writing this now.

But that's another entry.
